newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh hoped bomb would spark uprising - witness.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh hoped bomb would spark uprising - witness.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh plotted to blow up the Oklahoma City federal building to avenge the deaths of 80 cult members at Waco and spark a "general uprising" against the government, the prosecution's star witness testified on Monday.

Michael Fortier gave the most damning testimony so far in the trial of McVeigh, his former army buddy who is charged with blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

Fortier described how McVeigh's rage over the deadly end to the 1993 federal siege of the Branch Davidian cult compound at Waco, Texas, led him to plot the Oklahoma City attack exactly two years later.

Fortier, 28, said McVeigh and alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols singled out the Oklahoma City federal building because they believed, wrongly, that was where the order for the Waco raid came from. Nichols will be tried separately later.

McVeigh, who believed the U.S. government had declared war on the American people, wanted to "cause a general uprising in America, hopefully that would knock some people off the fence ... and urge them into taking action against the federal government," Fortier told chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler.

Fortier has pleaded guilty to four felony counts in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing but did nothing to stop it. He is in federal prison awaiting sentencing and faces up to 23 years in prison.
Asked by Hartzler if he realised he could have stopped the bombing with a phone call to authorities, Fortier replied: "I live with that knowledge every day, sir."

In a hard-hitting cross-examination, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones tried to undermine Fortier's credibility, painting him as a drug-taking financial failure with few prospects who saw a chance to make money by selling his story about McVeigh.
Jones stressed that Fortier's eventual sentence depended on how well he cooperated in his testimony. "It's a Sword of Damocles hanging over your head?" Jones said.
"It's their (prosecutors') sole discretion," Fortier agreed.

Fortier was on the witness stand for all but 10 minutes of the day and Jones was set to continue his cross-examination on Tuesday. The closely-watched trial has progressed far more quickly than expected and the prosecution is expected to wrap up its case as early as next week.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

Fortier testified that McVeigh was so determined to blow up the federal building he was prepared to risk killing himself. He told the court that McVeigh once told him he planned to stay in the explosives-packed truck to make sure it ignited, and would carry a gun with him to "blow away" anyone who interfered.
"Now you're talking about committing suicide. This is stupid," Fortier recalled telling McVeigh. When he heard about the bombing, Fortier said his first thought was: "Oh my God ... he did it."

McVeigh, who served with Fortier in the army and later came to live near him in Kingman, Arizona, told Fortier about the bombing plan in 1994 but Fortier told him he wanted no part of it, Fortier testified.

Despite his damaging testimony, Fortier told Hartzler: "If you don't consider what happened in Oklahoma, Tim is a good person." Jurors listened attentively to Fortier. McVeigh, who was the best man at Fortier's wedding, sometimes scowled but otherwise showed little emotion.

Under cross-examination, Fortier acknowledged he had sometimes mentioned the possibility of selling his story, once telling a friend: "I'm going to wait until after the trial to do movie and book rights." Fortier said earlier on Monday that he was not serious about selling his story.
He admitted lying to FBI agents as late as mid-May 1995.
Fortier answered Jones politely, but looked nervous, repeatedly drinking cups of water.

Fortier acknowledged he had been taking drugs, including crystal methamphetamine and marijuana, during the period of his alleged conversations with McVeigh and that he sold drugs in Kingman to help make ends meet.

Earlier, Fortier said McVeigh told him "he had figured out how to make a truck into a bomb". He described how McVeigh pointed out the target building when they both drove to Oklahoma City in late 1994.

When Fortier asked McVeigh if he was concerned about people in the building, McVeigh said they were like the stormtroopers in the "Star Wars" movies, Fortier said. They may be individually innocent but "they were part of the Evil Empire and were guilty by association," Fortier said McVeigh told him.
